checkpoints: Draw a diagram of how the browser, React app, Flask API, and database relate
Understand what CORS is and why it exists
Identify what runs on the client and what runs on the server
Set up a project folder with separate frontend/ and backend/ directories

content.value: A full stack app has two distinct programs: a React frontend that runs in the browser, and a Flask backend that runs on a server. They communicate over HTTP — React fetches data from Flask endpoints using the browser's fetch API or a library like axios. CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser security policy that blocks requests from one origin (localhost:5173) to another (localhost:5000) unless the server explicitly allows it. Install Flask-CORS: from flask_cors import CORS; CORS(app). Keep your frontend and backend in separate folders with separate dependencies.

checkpoints: Scaffold the React project with Vite in frontend/
Create a Flask app with a virtual environment in backend/
Start both dev servers simultaneously in two terminals
Make a test fetch from React to a Flask health check endpoint

content.value: Run both servers simultaneously: React on port 5173 (Vite default) and Flask on port 5000. In your React app, fetch from the Flask API: fetch('http://localhost:5000/api/health'). Your Flask health check returns { status: 'ok' }. If you see a CORS error, ensure Flask-CORS is configured. This first successful cross-origin request is the moment your full stack comes alive. Add a proxy in vite.config.js to avoid CORS during development: server.proxy['/api'] = 'http://localhost:5000'. With the proxy, React can call /api/health without the full origin.

checkpoints: Create a Flask route that returns a list of items as JSON
Fetch the list from React using useEffect and useState
Render the list in the browser
Handle loading and error states in the UI

content.value:
The core full stack loop: Flask returns JSON, React fetches and renders it. In Flask: @app.route('/api/items') returns jsonify([{'id': 1, 'name': 'Apple'}]). In React: useEffect(() => { fetch('/api/items').then(r => r.json()).then(setItems) }, []). Render with items.map(item =>
  • {item.name}
    • ). Display a loading spinner while fetching and an error message if the fetch fails. This pattern — fetch on mount, manage loading/error state, render results — is the full stack's heartbeat.

moduleTitle: Sending Data from React to Flask
checkpoints: Build a form in React with controlled inputs
Submit the form with a POST fetch to a Flask route
Read the JSON body in Flask and save to SQLite
Update the React list immediately after a successful POST

content.value: Writing data back to the server completes the loop. On form submit, send a POST with Content-Type: application/json and a JSON body: fetch('/api/items', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ name }) }). Flask reads it with request.get_json(). After a successful save, update the local state in React by appending the new item — this gives instant feedback without a full refetch. Optimistic updates (updating state before the server confirms) are the next level, but start with the simple pattern: wait for the response, then update.

checkpoints: Add a delete button to each list item in React
Send a DELETE request to Flask on button click
Remove the item from React state after successful deletion
Add an edit form that sends a PUT request

content.value: Delete is a DELETE request to /api/items/<id>. In React: fetch('/api/items/' + id, { method: 'DELETE' }). On success (204 No Content), filter the item out of state: setItems(items.filter(i => i.id !== id)). Edit is trickier: show an inline form pre-filled with the item's current values, submit a PUT request with the updated body, and on success replace the item in state. Notice the pattern: the HTTP method changes but the data flow (request → Flask processes → React updates state) stays the same.

checkpoints: Flask API with CRUD endpoints for to-do items
React frontend that fetches, creates, updates, and deletes items
SQLite database for persistence
Loading and error states handled in the UI
Deploy the Flask API and the React frontend

content.value: Your capstone is a complete, deployed full stack app. The Flask API handles persistence via SQLite, the React frontend consumes the API. Deploy Flask to Render (free tier) and React to Vercel (free tier). Update the API base URL in React to point to the deployed Flask URL. Test the deployed app end-to-end. Having a live, publicly accessible full stack app is a compelling portfolio piece that demonstrates you understand the entire development cycle — from local development through deployment.
